profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a civic-tech nonprofit that maintains an open-source COVID-19 exposure and case-trend platform used by two county health departments. Since Monday's release, the dashboard's county-level 'active cases' tiles have intermittently spiked and then dropped, and operators also noticed delayed exposure-notification syncs overnight. The issue appears somewhere between the nightly ingestion pipeline, layered caching, and the logic that merges revised public-health feeds. The agenda is to compare symptoms, narrow down the likely root cause, and agree on a same-day mitigation plus a short follow-up fix. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan, an owner for the immediate patch, and a decision on what evidence will count as the issue being fixed.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Distributed services, ETL pipelines, PostgreSQL performance, API caching
members.background: Priya joined the nonprofit after working on data infrastructure for a health analytics vendor and now owns the ingestion service that normalizes county CSV feeds, computes dashboard aggregates, and publishes API-ready results.
members.private_state: She wants to contain the incident without rolling back the release because a rollback would also remove a separate performance improvement she has been pushing for; she is especially worried that the ingestion job may be blamed when she suspects the visible spikes are mostly caused by application-side cache behavior around revised aggregates.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the cache update,' they mean the Redis cache-key versioning and invalidation behavior introduced with the new aggregate path, not infrastructure TTL settings.
A 'cache invalidation issue' most naturally points to application logic serving mismatched aggregate rows under fresh keys after county revisions, not to ingress behavior.

A 'fix' for this incident means restoring stable public dashboard numbers for the currently affected counties within the next ingestion cycle, even if historical backfill remains inconsistent until later.
Saying they should 'replay yesterday's data' naturally means rerunning the ETL from the sanitized snapshots already stored in S3, because that is the normal way to isolate the transformation layer.
If the dashboard remains flat after the next scheduled run, that is strong enough evidence that the customer-visible problem has been addressed for today.

members.name: Jonah Feldman
members.expertise: Production incident response, Kubernetes operations, observability, deployment safety
members.background: Jonah came from a telemedicine platform and now oversees runtime reliability, alerting, and release coordination for the nonprofit's public APIs, ingress layer, and worker services.
members.private_state: He wants to reduce user-visible instability and avoid another overnight page; he is open to a partial rollback if that lowers operational risk, and he is concerned the team may underweight platform-level symptoms because the dashboard anomalies are more visible than the sync-worker lag.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the cache update,' they mean the ingress cache TTL and eviction behavior changed during the rollout, because that is the cache layer most likely to create intermittent public spikes.
A 'cache invalidation issue' most naturally refers to stale responses being retained or evicted inconsistently by the ingress/controller layer under memory pressure, not to application code paths.
A 'fix' means the incident is not fixed until the API, dashboard, and exposure-sync worker all stop producing anomalies across at least a full day of scheduled jobs and alerts return to baseline.
If they agree to 'replay yesterday's data,' that means reprocessing from the raw landing bucket or original county feed endpoints so fetch timing and upstream revisions remain in scope.
One calm dashboard cycle is encouraging but not sufficient; the issue is only really resolved after overnight jobs and operational alerts behave normally.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the cache update' as the likely place the regression started.

misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jonah means the infrastructure-layer ingress cache TTL and eviction configuration changed during the rollout.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in a system with multiple cache layers and routinely shorten discussion to 'the cache' because everyone knows caching was touched on Monday; the shared phrase feels precise enough in context even though each defaults to the layer they own.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'fix it today' or have it 'stable by tonight.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya believes success means the county dashboard no longer shows visible spikes after the next pipeline run, even if historical consistency and the sync-worker issue remain for later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jonah believes success means all correlated symptoms are quiet through a full cycle of jobs and alerts, including the exposure-sync delays.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use 'fixed' and 'stable' conversationally during incidents without defining exit criteria, especially when both are trying to sound pragmatic and action-oriented rather than procedural.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'replay yesterday's data' to verify the hypothesis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya intends to rerun the ETL using the sanitized S3 snapshots that feed the aggregate job, which isolates the transformation layer.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jonah intends to replay from the raw landing bucket or original county endpoints to include fetch timing and upstream revisions in the test.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Replaying data is a routine operational phrase, and each person's default tooling makes their interpretation feel obviously implied; the difference hides in execution details rather than in the apparent plan.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the symptoms 'look like a cache invalidation issue' and move on as if they share the same root-cause hypothesis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya presupposes this means aggregate rows are being recomputed correctly but old application keys are dropped or replaced out of order, so some requests mix revised counts with newly generated cache entries.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jonah presupposes this means the ingress/controller layer is serving stale or inconsistently evicted responses because cache entries are aging out unevenly under memory pressure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, naming a broad failure mode often functions as enough shared grounding to proceed; because both explanations plausibly produce spikes and drops, neither feels a need to unpack which layer the phrase refers to.
